The Crucial disk now has one ext4 partition labelled `nexus-data`; I verified that `/dev/sda`’s partition table is unchanged. The public MicroVM modules are committed, and the first host-plus-VM build is downloading dependencies.

The configuration keeps DHCP on the physical Ethernet interface and assigns only the VM’s TAP interface to networkd.

       networkConfig = {          DHCP = \"no\";          LinkLocalAddressing = \"no\";          IPv6AcceptRA = false;        };      };      # Resolve the guest's named storage request to this host's backing path.      microvm.shares = [{        tag = \"test-data\";  systemd.services.\"microvm-virtiofsd@test-vm\".unitConfig.RequiresMountsFor = [ \"/srv/nexus-storage\" ];}NIXcat > vms/test-vm/default.nix <<'NIX'{ pkgs, ... }:{  networking.hostName = \"test-vm\";  networking.firewall.allowedTCPPorts = [ 8080 ];  systemd.services.test-data-init = {    description = \"Write a persistence marker from inside test-vm\";    wantedBy = [ \"multi-user.target\" ];    before = [ \"test-http.service\" ];    unitConfig.RequiresMountsFor = [ \"/data\" ];    serviceConfig = {      Type = \"oneshot\";      RemainAfterExit = true;    };    script = ''      set -eu      if [ "'! -e /data/persistence-proof.txt ]; then        printf '"'Nexus test-vm persistent data; first boot: %s\\n' \""'$(cat /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id)" > /data/persistence-proof.txt      fi      mkdir -p /run/test-vm      ln -s /data/persistence-proof.txt /run/test-vm/persistence-proof.txt      cat /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id > /run/test-vm/boot-id.txt      cp /etc/test-vm-revision /run/test-vm/revision.txt      printf '"'test-vm is running\\n' > /run/test-vm/index.html    '';  };  systemd.services.test-http = {    description = \"Host-only test HTTP service\";    wantedBy = [ \"multi-user.target\" ];    requires = [ \"test-data-init.service\" ];    after = [ \"test-data-init.service\" \"network-online.target\" ];    wants = [ \"network-online.target\" ];    serviceConfig = {      DynamicUser = true;      ExecStart = \""'${pkgs.python3}/bin/python -m http.server 8080 --bind 10.80.0.2 --directory /run/test-vm";      Restart = "on-failure";      NoNewPrivileges = true;      ProtectSystem = "strict";      ProtectHome = true;      PrivateTmp = true;    };  };}NIXcat > hosts/test-host/storage.nix <<'"'NIX'{ ... }:{  # Provisioned once as GPT + one ext4 partition on the Crucial SSD.  fileSystems.\"/srv/nexus-storage\" = {    device = \"/dev/disk/by-id/ata-CT500MX500SSD1_1840E1D099EF-part1\";    fsType = \"ext4\";    options = [ \"noatime\" ];  };}NIXsed -i '/\\.\\/hardware-configuration.nix/a\\    ./storage.nix' hosts/test-host/configuration.nixsed -i '/hardware.cpu.amd.updateMicrocode = true;/a\\  boot.kernelModules = [ \"kvm_amd\" ];' hosts/test-host/configuration.nixgit add flake.nix cluster vms hosts/test-hostnix flake update nexus-infranixos-rebuild build --flake /etc/nixos/Nexus-Infra-Private#test-hostROOTEOF"

Both Git repositories have no remote configured yet. The private input temporarily uses `git+file:///etc/nixos/Nexus-Infra?ref=main`; `flake.lock` pins a public commit. Commit public changes before updating this input. The public and upstream MicroVM inputs follow this deployment'"'s pinned NixOS 26.05 nixpkgs.## Layout- "'`hosts/test-host/`: physical host, hardware and storage mount.- `vms/test-vm/`: concrete guest requesting the named virtiofs filesystem `test-data`.- `cluster/test-host.nix`: VM placement, network addresses and mapping `test-data` to `/srv/nexus-storage/test-vm/test-data`.The host'"'s existing mutable account password stays outside Git. The authorized workstation **public** SSH key is declared in the host configuration. No passwords, private keys or other secrets belong in either repository.## Storage and networkingAMD SVM must be enabled in firmware. The host loads "'`kvm_amd`. `test-vm` uses QEMU/KVM with one vCPU and 256 MiB guest RAM, plus a read-only host Nix-store share.The Kingston `/dev/sda` layout is unchanged: EFI on `/dev/sda1`, root on `/dev/sda2`. The Crucial CT500MX500SSD1 (serial 1840E1D099EF) was provisioned once with GPT and one full-size ext4 partition, label `nexus-data`, UUID `9f013958-f0b2-48cd-a1d4-3da7c4a067ac`. NixOS mounts its stable by-id partition at `/srv/nexus-storage`. Rebuilds do not repartition or format anything. The VM and virtiofs daemon require this mount, and a storage preparation unit creates the declared share directory only after the mount is available. Data is not part of the guest'"'s disposable root filesystem.The host retains DHCP on "'`enp27s0`. Only the guest TAP `vm-test` is managed by networkd: host `10.80.0.1/30`, guest `10.80.0.2/30`. There is no LAN bridge, NAT, guest default route or public port forward. Guest HTTP listens on `10.80.0.2:8080`; the guest does not run SSH. The host can test HTTP, and Fedora can access it through an SSH tunnel.## Commands from FedoraBuild and activate the complete host and its declarative VM:```shssh -t nexus-test '"'sudo nixos-rebuild build --flake /etc/nixos/Nexus-Infra-Private#test-host'ssh -t nexus-test 'sudo nixos-rebuild switch --flake /etc/nixos/Nexus-Infra-Private#test-host'"'```Inspect, start, stop or restart the VM:```shssh nexus-test '"'systemctl --no-pager --full status microvm@test-vm.service'ssh -t nexus-test 'sudo systemctl start microvm@test-vm.service'ssh -t nexus-test 'sudo systemctl stop microvm@test-vm.service'ssh -t nexus-test 'sudo systemctl restart microvm@test-vm.service'ssh -t nexus-test 'sudo journalctl -u microvm@test-vm.service -u microvm-virtiofsd@test-vm.service -n 100 --no-pager'ssh nexus-test 'curl -fsS http://10.80.0.2:8080/; curl -fsS http://10.80.0.2:8080/persistence-proof.txt'ssh nexus-test 'findmnt /srv/nexus-storage; lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,MODEL,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS'"'```Optional browser access (leave the tunnel running, then open http://127.0.0.1:18080):```shssh -N -L 127.0.0.1:18080:10.80.0.2:8080 nexus-test```The guest writes `/data/persistence-proof.txt` on its first boot only. HTTP `/boot-id.txt` shows the current guest boot and `/revision.txt` identifies the guest build. Change the revision in `vms/test-vm/default.nix`, rebuild/switch the host, and compare these endpoints: boot/revision change while the persistence file stays identical. The guest writes this file itself; the host does not seed it.After editing public modules, commit them there, then update the private lock and rebuild:```shssh -t nexus-test '"'sudo bash -c \"cd /etc/nixos/Nexus-Infra-Private && nix flake update nexus-infra\"'"'```## GitHub setup still neededCreate/confirm the real `Nexus-Infra` public and `Nexus-Infra-Private` private GitHub repositories, add their actual remote URLs on this host, and configure Git authentication outside Git. Push the public repository first. Replace the private flake'"'s local "'`nexus-infra` URL with that actual public remote, update its lock, build/switch and commit. Then push the private repository. I’ll use a private `10.80.0.0/24` bridge for the three VMs, keep their disk mappings in the private repository, and expose only ingress HTTP on the host’s LAN address. There are no Git remotes yet. The temporary local Git input is commit-pinned in `flake.lock`; commit public changes before running `nix flake update nexus-infra` in this repository. All components use the same pinned NixOS 26.05 package set.## Deployment| VM | Address | vCPUs | RAM | Service || --- | --- | --- | --- | --- || test-vm | 10.80.0.2 | 1 | 256 MiB | Test HTTP on 8080 || network-control | 10.80.0.3 | 1 | 512 MiB | Headscale on 8080 || ingress | 10.80.0.4 | 1 | 256 MiB | Traefik on 80 |All use QEMU/KVM, autostart, a read-only Nix-store share, and key-only SSH for `jonas`. AMD SVM must stay enabled in firmware. Guest SSH host keys persist in `vm-state`. The guest user has journal access but no passwordless sudo; on network-control, membership in the `headscale` group permits administration via its local Unix socket. The workstation public key is declared; private keys and account passwords are not in Git.`hosts/test-host/` describes the machine/backend; `vms/` describes concrete instances; `cluster/test-host.nix` maps them to storage and addresses. `vms/common.nix` contains deployment access policy and the runtime persistence check.## StorageThe Kingston system disk is unchanged: `/dev/sda1` is EFI, `/dev/sda2` is root. The Crucial CT500MX500SSD1, serial 1840E1D099EF, contains one 465.8 GiB ext4 partition labelled `nexus-data`, UUID `9f013958-f0b2-48cd-a1d4-3da7c4a067ac`, mounted by stable disk ID at `/srv/nexus-storage`.The disk was already repurposed in the previous pass. This pass preserved all Nexus data, verified the former Debian root/swap offsets have no detectable filesystem signatures, and removed the two obsolete Debian EFI entries. No formatting/repartitioning occurred in this pass. Rebuilds never format disks.A VM requests `nexus.persistence.<name>.mountPoint`; the private cluster supplies its `source` under the host-specific storage root. The public module generates virtiofs shares and orders startup after the backing mount and directory preparation. The guest never names a physical disk.| VM | Name | Guest mount | Directory relative to host storage root || --- | --- | --- | --- || test-vm | test-data | /data | test-vm/test-data || network-control | control-state | /var/lib/headscale | network-control/control-state || ingress | ingress-state | /var/lib/traefik | ingress/ingress-state || each VM | vm-state | /var/lib/nexus | VM-name/vm-state |Headscale'"'s SQLite database and generated Noise key live only in persistent runtime storage. Future Traefik state belongs in its persistent directory; no TLS certificates are configured. Each share has a non-secret "'`.nexus-persistence-proof` marker written from inside its VM. Physical Ethernet `enp27s0` remains on DHCP and is not attached to this bridge. This is a single-host foundation, not a cross-host overlay or migration implementation.Only network-control has a default route and outbound NAT, scoped to `10.80.0.3/32`; it uses the existing LAN resolver. Headscale fetches its standard upstream Tailscale DERP directory. Embedded DERP, MagicDNS, client DNS overrides, OIDC and public TLS are disabled. Headscale is running locally, but no Tailscale clients are enrolled. It coordinates eventual peers; ordinary VM traffic crosses the bridge directly. The current declarations already contain VM placement, addresses and storage mappings; systemd exposes VM state and resource accounting without logging into guests.

Implementation plan:

- **Model:** generate host/VM/storage/network inventory from the private Nix declarations, then attach live observations. Keep declared placement, observed state and stale/offline status distinct.
- **Backend:** a small Python host agent on each physical host, plus a Python aggregation API in `nexus-console`. Agents collect local metrics; the console never treats its own `/proc` as host data.
- **Boundary and privileges:** mutual TLS between console and agents. Agents run unprivileged, with a systemd policy allowing only explicitly listed VM actions. Initially, only `test-vm` is controllable; infrastructure VMs are protected.
- **Browser security:** generated runtime administrator credentials, expiring sessions, CSRF checks and strict request validation. No shell, file-editing or Nix-evaluation endpoint.
- **UI:** a purpose-built interface with cluster overview, workload controls, storage attachments, network topology and an action history. Plain JavaScript/CSS keeps deployment small.
- **Updates:** agents sample every five seconds; the console caches host results and browsers poll the cache. Offline hosts retain clearly marked stale observations.
- **Deployment:** a persistent `nexus-console` VM behind the existing ingress at `/console/`. Adding hosts means declaring another inventory and authenticated agent endpoint, not redesigning the UI.

I’ll document this design in the repositories and proceed.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
  # Run ON test-host, normally via: ssh -At nexus-test 'bash /etc/nixos/Nexus-Infra-Private/scripts/verify.sh --restart'
  set -euo pipefail
  [[ $(hostname) == test-host ]] || { echo 'Run this script on nexus-test.' >&2; exit 1; }
  [[ -S ${SSH_AUTH_SOCK:-/nonexistent} ]] || { echo 'Forward your workstation SSH agent with ssh -A.' >&2; exit 1; }
  [[ ${1:-} == '' || ${1:-} == --restart ]] || { echo 'Usage: verify.sh [--restart]' >&2; exit 1; }
  sudo -v
  [[ $(findmnt -n -o SOURCE /) == /dev/sda2 ]]
  [[ $(findmnt -n -o SOURCE /boot) == /dev/sda1 ]]
  [[ $(findmnt -n -o SOURCE /srv/nexus-storage) == /dev/sdb1 ]]
  [[ $(lsblk -dn -o MODEL /dev/sdb | xargs) == CT500MX500SSD1 ]]
  sudo efibootmgr | grep -E '^BootCurrent:|^BootOrder:|^Boot[0-9A-F]{4}\* (Linux Boot Manager|UEFI OS)'
  if sudo efibootmgr | grep -qi debian; then echo 'Obsolete Debian boot entry found' >&2; exit 1; fi
  sudo wipefs --no-act /dev/sdb /dev/sdb1
  probe_dir=$(mktemp -d /tmp/nexus-validation.XXXXXX)
  printf 'Evidence directory: %s\n' "$probe_dir"
  ssh_opts=(-o BatchMode=yes -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new -o ConnectTimeout=3)
  declare -A ips=([test-vm]=10.80.0.2 [network-control]=10.80.0.3 [ingress]=10.80.0.4)
  declare -A services=([test-vm]=test-http [network-control]=headscale [ingress]=traefik)
  for vm in test-vm network-control ingress; do
    ip=${ips[$vm]}
    systemctl is-active "microvm@$vm.service" "microvm-virtiofsd@$vm.service" "microvm-storage-$vm.service"
    ssh "${ssh_opts[@]}" "jonas@$ip" "systemctl is-active sshd nexus-persistence-proof ${services[$vm]}"
    ssh "${ssh_opts[@]}" "jonas@$ip" 'cat /run/nexus-proof/*.txt' > "$probe_dir/$vm.before"
    ssh "${ssh_opts[@]}" "jonas@$ip" 'cat /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id' > "$probe_dir/$vm.boot-before"

# Nexus Console
  A lightweight cluster console with separate host agents. Python standard-library services and a static JavaScript/CSS frontend avoid a large dependency stack.
  ## Architecture
  A deployment supplies one inventory record per physical host, generated from the same declarations that create its VMs. The record contains VM identities, resource allocations, roles, network identities, persistent-directory attachments and permitted controls. No credentials belong in these records.
  Each unprivileged host agent observes `/proc`, systemd accounting, mounted-filesystem capacity, actual MicroVM units, runner symlinks, interfaces and declared HTTP readiness endpoints. Samples are cached every five seconds. The console polls hosts concurrently with bounded fan-out and serves cached observations to browsers. Known but unavailable hosts remain visible with stale data marked explicitly. Inventory represents the activated deployment, not uncommitted Git edits. Per-VM CPU is measured in core-percent and memory includes the hypervisor's host cgroup overhead.
  Agents require client certificates and verified TLS. Host certificate identities are checked, and agent responses must match their configured host ID and schema. A cluster CA can issue separate identities for additional physical hosts; adding them requires inventory, an endpoint and provisioning their certificates. This implements collection/placement visibility, not scheduling or migration.
  ## API and authority
  - Agent: `GET /v1/state`; `POST /v1/vms/{id}/actions` with exactly `{"action":"start|stop|restart"}`.
  - Console: `/console/api/v1/session`, `/state`, `/logout`, `/hosts/{host}/vms/{vm}/actions`.
  - Host IDs, VM IDs and actions are validated against configuration. There is no shell/file/Nix/SSH endpoint.
  - The agent account receives only per-unit start/stop/restart authority through polkit. It has no root account, sudo rule, disk-writing capability or guest-state read permission.
  - The console receives only an agent client identity. Its process cannot access the host bus or an SSH key.
  - Browser authentication uses a runtime-generated administrator password, a salted scrypt verifier, expiring HttpOnly/SameSite sessions, Host/Origin validation, and a session CSRF token. Login attempts, request sizes, worker counts and action rates are bounded.
  - Accepted actions are recorded in the console's persistent SQLite audit log and the host journal. An accepted action is not reported as completed until subsequent live observations change.
  - Agent TLS credentials and the console password are generated at runtime, outside Git and the Nix store. Browser transport is selected by the deployment; a plain-HTTP LAN deployment should use an SSH tunnel on an untrusted network.
  ## Deliberate limits
  One administrator, no roles or shared session storage; in-memory sessions expire on service restart. No historical metrics store. Volume attachments share backend capacity; per-directory consumption is not measured. Certificate rotation and host enrollment are manual. No automatic failover, relocation, or configuration editing. Retrieve the generated console password interactively (this is a distinct runtime credential):"'```shssh -t nexus-test '"'sudo cat /srv/nexus-storage/nexus-console/console-state/initial-password'"'```Browser transport is plain HTTP for this local test. On a network you do not trust, use the existing SSH trust relationship:```shssh -N -L 18080:10.80.0.5:8080 nexus-test# Open http://127.0.0.1:18080/console/```The tunnel terminates on test-host; traffic to the console crosses the host-local bridge. The console accepts only the explicitly configured LAN and tunnel origins. Do not publish this HTTP endpoint on the Internet.## Architecture and ownership`cluster/test-host.nix` remains the placement/address/storage source of truth. It generates inventory from the evaluated MicroVM declarations, including resource allocations and named persistent mounts. The host agent and console receive the same inventory. This is **activated desired state**, not a view of pending Git changes. Live status comes from the owning host agent. Known but unreachable hosts remain visible with stale observations labeled. Unexpected loaded MicroVM units are shown as undeclared and cannot be controlled.- `nexus-console`: 1 vCPU, 512 MiB RAM, private `10.80.0.5`, HTTP 8080.- Traefik in `ingress` routes `/console` and `/console/…` to the console. Existing `/` continues to proxy `test-vm`.- A small Python standard-library console API aggregates authenticated host snapshots; plain JavaScript/CSS renders the interface. No frontend build tool or external asset CDN.- Each host samples `/proc`, systemd cgroup accounting/unit state, filesystem capacity, runner identity, interfaces and explicit HTTP probes every five seconds. The console polls hosts concurrently (at most 32 requests) and browsers poll its cache every five seconds while visible. No per-browser host polling, metrics database or recursive disk scans.- `console-state` maps to `/srv/nexus-storage/nexus-console/console-state`, mounted at `/var/lib/nexus-console`. It retains authentication verifier, generated password, client identity and SQLite action audit. The separate `vm-state` retains guest SSH identity.- Named storage still means guest logical request → private mapping → local persistent filesystem. No distributed storage or migration is introduced.Add future physical hosts by declaring their inventory and agent URL, provisioning host server identities under the management CA, and allowing the console on their private management network. Every observation/action is addressed by host ID plus VM ID. Certificate enrollment and network transport across hosts remain manual. Scheduling and placement mutation are deliberately absent.## API and privilegesConsole endpoints under `/console/api/v1`:| Method | Path | Purpose ||---|---|---|| POST | `/session` | Login with runtime password || GET | `/session` | Restore session and obtain CSRF token || GET | `/state` | Cached inventory, observations and recent audit events || POST | `/hosts/{host}/vms/{vm}/actions` | Exactly `{"action":"start"}`, `stop`, or `restart` || POST | `/logout` | Revoke browser session |Only `test-vm` is controllable in this deployment. Confirmation is required in the UI; jobs return accepted and subsequent observations confirm completion. Timeouts never automatically retry a mutation. Stopping an autostart VM shows divergence without changing Nix configuration.The agent listens at `10.80.0.1:9443` with mutual TLS. The host firewall permits the console source IP only. An unprivileged `nexus-agent` account receives polkit permission only for start/stop/restart of `microvm@test-vm.service`; it cannot manage SSH, ingress or other host units. The unprivileged console service has neither host SSH credentials nor host systemd access. Both services have systemd filesystem/device/capability restrictions. Runtime certificate private keys never enter Git or the Nix store.Browser authentication uses a salted scrypt verifier, expiring HttpOnly/SameSite cookies, Host/Origin checks and a per-session CSRF token. Request bodies, supported actions, object IDs, concurrent connections and action rates are bounded. Sessions are deliberately invalidated when the service restarts. One administrator is supported; there is no user/role management yet.## Fedora commands```sh# Reproduce and activate the pinned deployment; sudo prompts on the remote host.ssh -t nexus-test '"'sudo nixos-rebuild build --flake /etc/nixos/Nexus-Infra-Private#test-host'ssh -t nexus-test 'sudo nixos-rebuild switch --flake /etc/nixos/Nexus-Infra-Private#test-host'# Host services and VM statusssh nexus-test 'systemctl status nexus-agent microvm@nexus-console --no-pager'ssh -t nexus-test 'sudo journalctl -u nexus-agent -u microvm@nexus-console -n 100 --no-pager'ssh -t nexus-test 'sudo systemctl restart microvm@nexus-console'ssh -t nexus-test 'sudo systemctl restart nexus-agent'# Guest service logs/status (ProxyJump uses the Fedora SSH key, no key copied to host)ssh -J nexus-test jonas@10.80.0.5 'systemctl status nexus-console --no-pager'ssh -J nexus-test jonas@10.80.0.5 'journalctl -u nexus-console -n 100 --no-pager'# Existing workload controls and LAN pathsssh -t nexus-test 'sudo systemctl restart microvm@test-vm'curl -fsS http://192.168.178.192:8080/curl -fsS http://192.168.178.192:8080/console/healthz# Full existing cluster/persistence verifier (restarts all four guests)ssh -At nexus-test 'bash /etc/nixos/Nexus-Infra-Private/scripts/verify.sh --restart'# Console API checks; add --restart to exercise test-vm lifecycle and persistencessh -t nexus-test 'sudo nix shell /nix/store/pnl8li8q1bvaq6hr5y3mfdqhyjvsqwk6-source#python3 -c python3 /etc/nixos/Nexus-Infra-Private/scripts/verify-console.py --restart'"'````verify-console.py` reads the runtime password locally as root and never prints it. `verify.sh` uses temporary SSH agent forwarding for guest checks; ordinary administration can use ProxyJump instead.## Runtime credentials and maintenanceThe private `cluster/console-pki.nix` oneshot generates the cluster CA, host server certificate and console client certificate at first deployment. CA and server keys stay in `/var/lib/nexus-agent-pki` on the host; only the client identity and public CA enter the console'"'s persistent share. Leaf certificates expire after 365 days; CA after 3650 days. Enrollment/renewal is manual for this first version. Back up this runtime state securely, outside Git. Rebuilding restores configuration, not lost credentials or data.To rotate the administrator password, stop the console VM, remove only "'`auth.json` and `initial-password` from its `console-state` directory, and start it again. It generates a new random credential; audit history remains. Retrieve it using the command above. No application password is stored in a Nix expression.To renew leaf certificates using the existing CA, schedule a console outage, stop the console VM and agent, remove only `server.crt` and `client.crt` in `/var/lib/nexus-agent-pki`, restart `nexus-console-pki`, and start the agent and console VM. The oneshot creates new leaf keys/certificates and installs the new client identity in the persistent share. Do not remove `ca.key` or `ca.crt` during leaf renewal. Confirm health and login afterward.## Limitations and next steps- No historical metrics, per-directory storage accounting or quotas. VM process memory includes hypervisor overhead; CPU is percent of one logical core.- HTTP probes check endpoint availability, not all guest services. Topology shows declared paths rather than packet tracing.- Current desired/live comparison covers placement, autostart and runner identity, not uncommitted/unactivated Git changes.- Audit captures accepted or unconfirmed permitted actions, not a comprehensive security event stream. There is one shared administrator identity.- No multi-host transport, automated enrollment, automatic certificate rotation, migrations, failover or scheduling yet.- Next steps: browser HTTPS and individual identities/roles, certificate lifecycle, a second host to exercise placement visibility, then reviewed desired-state workflows.- Neither repository has a configured GitHub remote. Local Git dependency remains pinned and working; create/configure the public and private remotes before replacing it. Never reverse the private → public dependency.MDsudo -n bash -s <<'"'ROOT'cat >> /etc/nixos/Nexus-Infra-Private/README.md <<'MD'## Nexus ConsoleThe live cluster console is available at "'`http://192.168.178.192:8080/console/`.See [CONSOLE.md](CONSOLE.md) for authentication, architecture, API, security boundaries and exact Fedora administration commands. The console is itself a declarative MicroVM with persistent runtime credentials and audit history.MDROOTEOF'

#!/nix/store/axl12yr00f105bjqvj628f5f0s6r0cnp-bash-5.3p9/bin/bash
  # Exit gracefully if QEMU is already gone (e.g., killed by machinectl)
  if [ ! -S nexus-console.sock ]; then
    exit 0
  fi
  # Use ACPI power button. A Ctrl+Alt+Del via input-send-event needs a keyboard,
  # which headless guests do not have: QEMU rejects it with "Input handler not
  # found for event type key", so the guest never stops, only gets killed after
  # the timeout.
  (
    echo '{"execute":"qmp_capabilities"}'
    echo '{"execute":"system_powerdown"}'
  ) | \
  /nix/store/p2k79yam5dw1mhac4h9ixw4mxkh0gvjw-socat-1.8.1.3/bin/socat STDIO UNIX:nexus-console.sock,shut-none
  # Wait for the guest to actually shut down.
  # Probing the socket instead of reading stdin makes the wait independent
  # of how this script was invoked. QEMU stops accepting connections on the
  # QMP socket once it exits, so a failing connect is the signal that it is
  # gone.
  while /nix/store/p2k79yam5dw1mhac4h9ixw4mxkh0gvjw-socat-1.8.1.3/bin/socat -u /dev/null UNIX:nexus-console.sock 2>/dev/null; do
    sleep 1
  done

The console provides live host metrics, VM placement/status, storage attachments, network topology, service health, and action history.

- **Architecture:** lightweight Python backend and host agent, with plain JavaScript/CSS frontend. Inventory comes from existing Nix declarations; live observations come from each physical host.
- **Updates:** five-second cached polling, with explicit stale/offline states.
- **Security:** authenticated browser sessions, CSRF/Origin checks, mutual TLS between console and agent, unprivileged services, and narrowly scoped polkit permissions.
- **Controls:** start, stop, and restart `test-vm`. Infrastructure VMs remain protected.
- **Multi-host path:** add host inventories, agent endpoints, and certificates. No scheduling or migration was introduced.

| VM | Private IP | Allocation |
|---|---|---|
| test-vm | 10.80.0.2 | 1 vCPU / 256 MiB |
| network-control | 10.80.0.3 | 1 vCPU / 512 MiB |
| ingress | 10.80.0.4 | 1 vCPU / 256 MiB |
| nexus-console | 10.80.0.5 | 1 vCPU / 512 MiB |

Ingress routes `/console/` to the console; `/` still reaches test-vm. Console credentials, TLS identity, and audit history persist on the existing Nexus storage disk.

The management API exposes authenticated state/session endpoints and an allowlisted VM-action endpoint under `/console/api/v1`. It exposes no shell, file editor, or arbitrary commands.

**Validation passed:** committed configuration builds and switches; all four VMs are healthy; browser start/stop/restart works; offline recovery works; persistence survived console replacement and workload restarts. Fedora-to-ingress connectivity passed. No failed systemd units remain.

At minimum search for:
- passwords
- API tokens
- private keys
- LAN-specific private deployment data
- my sudo password
- private repository paths that reveal unnecessary deployment details
- credentials
- host-specific UUIDs
- host-specific secrets

Also inspect `.gitignore`.

Add an appropriate `.gitignore` where useful.

Do the same security check for Nexus-Infra-Private even though it is private.

A private repository is NOT permission to commit plaintext secrets.

Do not push if sensitive material is found until it is removed appropriately.

COMMIT STRUCTURE
================

Create coherent commits.

Examples of reasonable separation:

Nexus-Infra:
- Configure public repository metadata/docs
- Document Nexus architecture

Nexus-Infra-Private:
- Point deployment at GitHub Nexus-Infra
- Add private deployment documentation

Use judgment based on actual changes.

Do not squash existing useful history unnecessarily.

VALIDATION
==========

Before finishing:

1. Verify local GitHub authentication.
2. Verify agent-forwarded GitHub authentication from nexus-test.
3. Verify both GitHub repository visibilities.
4. Verify both origins.
5. Verify both branches track origin/main.
6. Verify all intended commits are pushed.
7. Verify Nexus-Infra is public.
8. Verify Nexus-Infra-Private is private.
9. Verify no secrets were committed.
10. Verify private flake references the GitHub-hosted Nexus-Infra.
11. Run:

    ssh nexus-test \
      "printf '%s\n' '1234' | sudo -S nixos-rebuild build --flake /etc/nixos/Nexus-Infra-Private#test-host"

12. Confirm the build succeeds.

Do not modify unrelated local Fedora repositories or Git configuration.

FINAL REPORT
============

Report:

1. authenticated GitHub username
2. GitHub URLs for both repositories
3. confirmed visibility of each repository
4. Git identity configured
5. SSH authentication arrangement
6. whether agent forwarding is being used
7. origins configured
8. branches/upstreams
9. commits created
10. files/documentation added
11. final public repository tree
12. final private repository tree
13. result of secret/security scan
14. result of nixos-rebuild build
15. anything requiring manual action

I’ll check local GitHub authentication and forwarded access, then audit both repositories’ full history before any push. After that I’ll configure GitHub, document the implementation, update the flake dependency, and verify the build.

Does Hetzner allow me to install NixOS on one of their VPS?

Yes. Hetzner Cloud VPSs can run NixOS, even though NixOS isn't one of Hetzner's standard OS images.
Hetzner explicitly supports attaching ISO images—including custom ISOs—to Cloud servers. NixOS also has documented Hetzner Cloud installation methods.
The main options are:
- NixOS ISO: Mount the NixOS minimal ISO, boot through Hetzner's web console, and install normally. You'll need to account for Hetzner's manual network/gateway configuration during ISO installs.
- `nixos-anywhere`: Usually the nicer option. Create the VPS with something like Debian, then remotely replace it with NixOS using your Nix configuration.
- `nixos-infect`: Convert an existing Debian/Ubuntu installation into NixOS. It works, though I'd generally prefer `nixos-anywhere` for a fresh server.
Both Hetzner's x86 VPSs and their ARM64 CAX VPSs are viable; you just need a matching NixOS architecture. Hetzner uses KVM with VirtIO networking/storage, which NixOS supports normally.
For your existing Hetzner setup, NixOS + `nixos-anywhere` would actually be a particularly good fit if your goal is to make the entire VPS configuration—users, SSH, firewall, Docker/Podman, Traefik, Mailcow prerequisites, backups, etc.—reproducible from Git.

That was the idea. So your initial observation would be that NixOS is quite a good fit for what I'm trying to do?

Yes. For what you're trying to do, NixOS is unusually well suited.
Your VPS isn't just "a Linux box running one application." You're moving toward a small, integrated infrastructure: reverse proxy, multiple services, databases, authentication, mail, backups, firewall/network configuration, domains/certificates, and potentially more servers later. The valuable property of NixOS here is that the server itself becomes configuration-as-code, rather than just the applications running on it.
In particular, you could eventually have something conceptually like:
infrastructure/
├── flake.nix
├── hosts/
│   ├── production.nix
│   └── staging.nix
├── modules/
│   ├── traefik.nix
│   ├── mail.nix

│   ├── firewall.nix
│   └── monitoring.nix
└── secrets/
Then a new VPS becomes roughly "install NixOS → apply this repo → get my infrastructure." Rollbacks are also a major advantage: a bad system configuration creates a new NixOS generation rather than irreversibly modifying the existing environment.
The main downside is complexity. Nix/NixOS has a substantial learning curve, and software that assumes conventional Linux filesystem layouts or imperative installation can occasionally be annoying. Mailcow is the part I'd investigate most carefully because it is a large Docker-based appliance with fairly strong assumptions about its host.
But architecturally: yes, I'd prefer NixOS over Debian for the infrastructure you're describing, especially since maintaining the infrastructure itself is becoming part of your software project rather than merely a means of hosting it.

- arbitrary destructive disk operations

If configuration changes such as “move VM to another host” should eventually be possible, represent that in the architecture/design but do not necessarily implement it in this pass.


ARCHITECTURAL REQUIREMENT
=========================

Do NOT build the UI by scraping HTML or executing arbitrary shell commands received from the frontend.

Create a proper backend/service boundary.

Conceptually:

    browser
       |
       v
    Nexus Console frontend
       |
       v
    Nexus management API
       |
       +--> cluster state
       +--> MicroVM/systemd state
       +--> host metrics
       +--> storage state
       +--> network state
       +--> narrowly permitted actions

Determine a sensible implementation architecture yourself.

The console VM should receive only the privileges/capabilities it actually needs.

Think carefully about the fact that Nexus will eventually span multiple physical hosts.

A design that only works by reading `/proc` on the machine hosting the console is insufficient.

For this first version it is acceptable to implement the minimum infrastructure required for one host while defining a clean path toward multiple hosts.


DISCOVERY / STATE MODEL
=======================

Investigate how Nexus currently knows:

- which hosts exist
- which VMs exist
- VM -> host assignment
- persistent storage relationships
- network identities

Do not duplicate sources of truth unnecessarily.

Where possible:

- desired topology should originate from the existing Nix/private cluster declarations
- runtime status should originate from the actual running systems

Design a clean representation/API for combining these.


LIVE UPDATES
============

The console should feel live.

Choose an appropriate mechanism yourself, e.g. polling, SSE, WebSockets, or another simple method.

Avoid excessive polling or architecture that will become wasteful as the cluster grows.

The current cluster is tiny, but design with perhaps dozens of hosts/VMs in mind rather than thousands.


NEXUS UI DESIGN
===============

Design the UI yourself.

The UI should make it easy to answer at a glance:

- Is the Nexus cluster healthy?
- Which physical machines are active?
- What workloads are running?
- Where is each VM running?
- Is anything stopped or unhealthy?
- What storage is attached to what?
- How does traffic/networking flow through the system?
- What is consuming resources?

Use visualization where it materially improves understanding.

Do not merely create a table dump of `systemctl` output.

At the same time, avoid unnecessary visual gimmicks.

This is an infrastructure administration interface.


DEPLOYMENT
==========

The console itself must be a declaratively defined Nexus VM.

Reusable pieces belong in:

    Nexus-Infra

Concrete instance/deployment configuration belongs in:

    Nexus-Infra-Private

Follow the existing public/private distinction.

The console should run as part of the same MicroVM infrastructure as other Nexus workloads.

For the current local test system, make it reachable from my Fedora workstation over the LAN.

It does NOT need:
- public Internet exposure
- Cloudflare
- public DNS
- public TLS certificates

If it makes sense, route it through the existing local ingress. Otherwise expose it appropriately on the LAN and explain the decision.


SECURITY
========

Treat this as the beginning of a real infrastructure control plane.

Even though this is a LAN-only test:

- do not trust browser input
- validate API requests
- expose only explicit allowed actions
- do not expose arbitrary shell execution
- do not put secrets into frontend bundles
- do not put secrets into Git
- do not put secrets into the Nix store
- minimize privileges of the console VM/service

Authentication can remain simple for the LAN test if implementing full authentication would significantly distract from the architecture, but structure the system so authentication can be added cleanly.

If you believe authentication is necessary even for this test version, implement a reasonable minimal solution without embedding plaintext credentials in Git.


DO NOT IMPLEMENT YET
====================

Do not expand scope into:

- Kubernetes
- Nomad
- Grafana
- Prometheus unless there is an exceptionally strong reason
- generic monitoring stacks
- Cloudflare
- public DNS
- Mailcow
- Antragsbank
- unrelated application workloads
- distributed storage
- automatic failover/orchestration
- complex scheduling

The Nexus Console should gather only the data it needs using a lightweight purpose-built mechanism where practical.


DEVELOPMENT APPROACH
====================

First:

1. inspect current Nexus repos
2. inspect current MicroVM architecture
3. inspect current networking/storage abstractions
4. inspect what information is already declaratively available
5. inspect what runtime information can safely be exposed

Then DESIGN the console architecture.

Before coding, write a concise implementation plan explaining:

- data model
- backend architecture
- how host/runtime state is collected
- API boundary
- privilege model
- frontend approach
- live-update mechanism
- how this extends to multiple hosts

If you encounter a major architectural decision with significant long-term consequences, stop and ask me.

Otherwise proceed autonomously.


VALIDATION
==========

At the end, the following should work:

From Fedora I can open the Nexus Console in a browser.

The console correctly shows the current test cluster, including at least:

- test-host
- current Nexus VMs
- VM -> host relationships
- running/stopped state
- useful host resource information
- persistent storage relationships
- current relevant network information

At least one safe VM control should work end-to-end, e.g.:

    restart test-vm

The UI should update afterward and reflect reality.

Verify the cluster remains reproducibly buildable:

    ssh nexus-test \
      "printf '%s\n' '1234' | sudo -S nixos-rebuild build --flake /etc/nixos/Nexus-Infra-Private#test-host"

and switch when appropriate.

Do not leave the cluster in a broken state.


GIT
===

Commit coherent changes separately in Nexus-Infra and Nexus-Infra-Private.

Do not commit generated runtime data, credentials, tokens, passwords, or mutable VM state.

Do not push unless valid remotes/authentication already exist.


FINAL REPORT
============

Report:

1. architecture chosen for Nexus Console
2. frontend/backend technologies selected and why
3. final repository changes
4. new VM/resource allocation
5. management API structure
6. privilege/security model
7. how live host/VM/storage/network data is collected
8. how this design extends to multiple physical hosts
9. URL/address I can open from Fedora
10. controls implemented
11. tests performed
12. exact commands to inspect/restart/debug the console from Fedora
13. remaining limitations
14. logical next steps
The important architectural step here is that this begins creating an actual Nexus control plane API, rather than making a dashboard that happens to SSH into things. That API can later become the foundation for scheduling/migration, configuration changes, alerts, and eventually automated cluster management.

Yes. The cleanest setup is:
- Create `Nexus-Infra` as public
- Create `Nexus-Infra-Private` as private
- Use your Fedora machine's existing GitHub SSH key via SSH agent forwarding, rather than copying the private key onto `nexus-test`
- Configure Git author email as `jonas.hoerter@proton.me`
- Add proper `origin` remotes and push both repos
- Then do a documentation pass on the public repo
Give Codex this prompt:
Continue working on my Nexus infrastructure.

You are running on my local Fedora workstation.

The Nexus host is remote and is reached using:

    ssh nexus-test

Repositories currently live on the REMOTE host:

    /etc/nixos/Nexus-Infra
    /etc/nixos/Nexus-Infra-Private

The GitHub remotes are currently not configured.

GOALS
=====

This pass has two goals:

1. Fully configure Git/GitHub for both repositories and push them.
2. Perform a proper documentation pass, primarily on the public Nexus-Infra repository.

GITHUB ACCOUNT
==============

The Git author email should be:

    jonas.hoerter@proton.me

Use my normal GitHub account associated with the SSH credentials already present on my LOCAL Fedora machine.

Do NOT copy my SSH private key onto nexus-test.

Prefer SSH agent forwarding or local GitHub tooling.

Repository names must be:

    Nexus-Infra
    Nexus-Infra-Private

Visibility:

    Nexus-Infra          -> PUBLIC
    Nexus-Infra-Private  -> PRIVATE

Do not accidentally make Nexus-Infra-Private public.

SSH / AUTHENTICATION
====================

First inspect the LOCAL Fedora machine:

    git config --global --list
    ssh-add -l
    ls ~/.ssh
    ssh -T git@github.com

Do not print or inspect private key contents.

Determine whether GitHub SSH authentication already works locally.

Also inspect whether the `gh` CLI exists and is authenticated:

    gh --version
    gh auth status

If `gh` is authenticated, prefer using it to create/configure the GitHub repositories.

If `gh` is not authenticated but SSH Git access works:
- do not create new credentials
- determine whether repository creation can be done safely another way
- if repository creation itself requires interactive authentication that is unavailable, stop only for that specific manual step and tell me exactly what I need to do

REMOTE AUTHENTICATION
=====================

Git repositories themselves currently live on nexus-test.

Do NOT copy a private SSH key to nexus-test.

Prefer SSH agent forwarding.

Test whether this works:

    ssh -A nexus-test 'ssh -T git@github.com'

GitHub may return a non-zero exit status even when authentication succeeds, so interpret the actual message correctly.

If necessary, inspect my local SSH config and use ForwardAgent for nexus-test, but do not weaken unrelated SSH security.

The goal is that Git commands executed on nexus-test can authenticate to GitHub using the LOCAL Fedora SSH agent.

GIT IDENTITY
============

Configure both remote repositories with:

    user.name  = Jonas
    user.email = jonas.hoerter@proton.me

Prefer repository-local Git configuration unless there is a strong reason to modify global configuration on nexus-test.

Verify with:

    git config user.name
    git config user.email

Do not rewrite existing commits solely to change author metadata unless necessary.

REPOSITORY CREATION
===================

Create these GitHub repositories if they do not already exist:

PUBLIC:
    Nexus-Infra

PRIVATE:
    Nexus-Infra-Private

Use SSH remotes, not HTTPS.

Expected remote form:

    git@github.com:<actual-github-username>/Nexus-Infra.git
    git@github.com:<actual-github-username>/Nexus-Infra-Private.git

Discover the actual authenticated GitHub username rather than guessing it.

Do not hardcode a username based only on assumptions.

Configure:

    origin

for each remote repository.

Ensure the default branch is:

    main

Push all current commits and establish upstream tracking.

Afterward these should work on nexus-test:

    git status
    git remote -v
    git branch -vv
    git push

PUBLIC/PRIVATE DEPENDENCY
=========================

Once Nexus-Infra exists on GitHub, replace any temporary local Git dependency such as:

    git+file:///etc/nixos/Nexus-Infra

or equivalent local paths

with the proper GitHub flake input.

The private flake should consume the public repository through GitHub.

Do NOT create any dependency from Nexus-Infra back to Nexus-Infra-Private.

Update flake.lock appropriately.

Then verify:

    sudo nixos-rebuild build --flake /etc/nixos/Nexus-Infra-Private#test-host

Do not switch unless required by the changes.

REMOTE SUDO
===========

The temporary sudo password on nexus-test is:

    1234

If non-interactive sudo is required:

    printf '%s\n' '1234' | sudo -S <command>

Never store that password in:
- Git
- Nix files
- scripts
- environment files
- README files
- shell configuration
- commit messages

DOCUMENTATION PASS
==================

After GitHub is configured, inspect the CURRENT implementation thoroughly before documenting it.

Do not document features that do not actually exist.

The public Nexus-Infra repository should get a useful README.md aimed at:

1. someone trying to understand Nexus
2. a friend wanting to create their own Nexus deployment
3. a contributor trying to understand the public/private split

Design the documentation structure yourself.

At minimum, it should explain accurately:

- what Nexus is
- what problem it is trying to solve
- desired-state vs live-state distinction
- public Nexus-Infra vs private deployment repository
- physical hosts
- MicroVM workloads
- host modules
- VM modules
- persistent storage concept
- networking model
- ingress
- network-control component
- Nexus Console
- current limitations
- how a user's private deployment consumes Nexus-Infra
- how to build/rebuild a host
- basic repository layout

Include concise architecture diagrams where Markdown diagrams or Mermaid materially improve clarity.

Do not make the README bloated.

Prefer:
- concise explanations
- practical commands
- actual current architecture
- clear extension points

Avoid:
- marketing language
- pretending Nexus is production-ready
- invented features
- speculative promises

If additional focused documentation is useful, create a small `docs/` directory, but only where it materially improves comprehension.

Potential topics could include:
- architecture
- storage model
- networking
- creating a host
- creating a VM

Choose based on what currently exists.

PRIVATE DOCUMENTATION
=====================

Nexus-Infra-Private may have a concise README explaining:

- this repository is private deployment state
- host definitions
- VM instances
- cluster assignments
- private storage/network configuration
- secrets policy

Do not include secrets or sensitive values in documentation.

SECURITY / GIT HYGIENE
======================

Before the first public push of Nexus-Infra, inspect its entire tracked history/content for accidental sensitive information.

At minimum search for:
- passwords
- API tokens
- private keys
- LAN-specific private deployment data
- my sudo password
- private repository paths that reveal unnecessary deployment details
- credentials
- host-specific UUIDs
- host-specific secrets

Also inspect `.gitignore`.

Add an appropriate `.gitignore` where useful.

Do the same security check for Nexus-Infra-Private even though it is private.

A private repository is NOT permission to commit plaintext secrets.

Do not push if sensitive material is found until it is removed appropriately.

COMMIT STRUCTURE
================

Create coherent commits.

Examples of reasonable separation:

Nexus-Infra:
- Configure public repository metadata/docs
- Document Nexus architecture

Nexus-Infra-Private:
- Point deployment at GitHub Nexus-Infra
- Add private deployment documentation

Use judgment based on actual changes.

Do not squash existing useful history unnecessarily.

VALIDATION
==========

Before finishing:

1. Verify local GitHub authentication.
2. Verify agent-forwarded GitHub authentication from nexus-test.
3. Verify both GitHub repository visibilities.
4. Verify both origins.
5. Verify both branches track origin/main.
6. Verify all intended commits are pushed.
7. Verify Nexus-Infra is public.
8. Verify Nexus-Infra-Private is private.
9. Verify no secrets were committed.
10. Verify private flake references the GitHub-hosted Nexus-Infra.
11. Run:

    ssh nexus-test \
      "printf '%s\n' '1234' | sudo -S nixos-rebuild build --flake /etc/nixos/Nexus-Infra-Private#test-host"

12. Confirm the build succeeds.

Do not modify unrelated local Fedora repositories or Git configuration.

FINAL REPORT
============

Report:

1. authenticated GitHub username
2. GitHub URLs for both repositories
3. confirmed visibility of each repository
4. Git identity configured
5. SSH authentication arrangement
6. whether agent forwarding is being used
7. origins configured
8. branches/upstreams
9. commits created
10. files/documentation added
11. final public repository tree
12. final private repository tree
13. result of secret/security scan
14. result of nixos-rebuild build
15. anything requiring manual action
The key thing is SSH agent forwarding. Your Fedora key remains on Fedora, while commands executed through `ssh -A nexus-test` can temporarily use that agent to authenticate to GitHub. There is no reason to place a GitHub private key permanently on the server.
